articles.title: MLB power rankings: Brewers take No. 1 spot ahead of Braves and Dodgers in all-NL top 3; Rays and Phillies round out top 5
articles.summary: Our latest power rankings identify a realistic goal for each team over the final month of the regular season.
articles.body:
September is here, which means one more month of the regular season to whittle the field of 30 teams down to the 12 that will compete in the postseason. A little more than half of MLB's teams still have a realistic chance of playing in October , while the rest will be using the remaining 25 or so games to deploy their rosters with an eye toward the future.

Whether a team is pushing for home-field advantage or the final wild-card spot or easing off the gas to preserve health and perhaps draft lottery positioning , these final four weeks of games can be valuable. In this latest edition of our power rankings, we'll suggest a realistic goal and/or organizational focus for each team over the final month of the regular season.

Jump to a team by clicking on the links below:

AL Central: White Sox | Guardians | Twins | Tigers | Royals

NL Central: Brewers | Cubs | Cardinals | Pirates | Reds

Identify the postseason rotation. Jacob Misiorowski has established himself as one of the best pitchers on the planet. Logan Henderson has emerged as a worthy No. 2, posting a 2.36 ERA across nine starts since he was activated from the injured list on July 9. But then what? Who will get the ball in Games 3 and 4 in October? Kyle Harrison's August featured three gems against losing teams (Pirates, Mariners, Mets) and two complete disasters against quality ballclubs (Padres, Cubs). Shane Drohan and Robert Gasser have shown flashes but are rookies. Dustin May has been frustratingly inconsistent since arriving at the deadline. Milwaukee needs to spend September sorting through these arms and getting at least two on track before the postseason.

Secure a top-two seed. The Braves have some questions to answer at a few positions (shortstop, left field) and in the rotation behind Chris Sale. But their chances of going on a deep run in October will increase exponentially if they can avoid playing in the wild-card series and rest up before giving Sale the ball in NLDS Game 1 (for his long-awaited first postseason start as a Brave), rather than burning Sale in the opening round. Seizing the tiebreaker over the Dodgers with a statement sweep in Atlanta last week was a great first step, but there's more work to be done for the Braves to finish ahead in the standings.

Find some offensive momentum. For close to two months now, scoring runs has been a slog for the reigning champs. Since their 12-run outburst against San Diego on July 2, the Dodgers are hitting .241/.309/.380 across 49 games, amounting to a 90 wRC+ that ranks 24th in MLB over that span . That's hardly the production of a juggernaut lineup like the one that existed for the first 88 games of the season, when L.A. collectively hit .267/.349/.445, good for a 120 wRC+ that was tops league-wide by a mile.

Whatever the reasons behind the recent fall-off, the L.A. bats have a real opportunity to build some confidence over the final month against the easiest remaining schedule in the National League . Whether that will sufficiently prepare them for the gauntlet of arms that await in October is another question entirely, but it would be good for L.A. to put a few more crooked numbers on the scoreboard before their pursuit of a three-peat begins in earnest.

Clinch the top seed. The Rays have built a nice cushion atop the American League, thanks to their consistency and propensity to dominate series; taking all three from San Diego over the weekend marked Tampa Bay's MLB-leading 14th sweep of the year. They've also been excellent at Tropicana Field, heightening the incentive to claim home-field advantage throughout the bracket. As such, Tampa Bay should be motivated to rack up enough wins to secure the AL's No. 1 seed, ideally before they head out on the road for four games at the Yankees and three games at the Phillies in the final week of the regular season.

Clinch the top wild-card spot. The Phillies enter September four games back of Atlanta with seven games against the rival Braves left on the schedule, so perhaps Philadelphia still has a division crown in its sights. But if I'm offering a more realistic objective — especially with the Braves having won five of six against the Phillies so far this season, thus needing just two more wins to claim the tiebreaker — the focus should be on ensuring a wild-card series takes place at Citizens Bank Park. The Phillies have caught up to the Cubs atop the NL wild-card standings, so it'll be a race to earn hosting rights between the two clubs.

Clinch the top wild-card spot. See above. The Cubs occupy a similar space as the Phillies, with an even smaller chance of chasing down the division-leading Brewers but in strong position to guarantee some postseason home games. Chicago's resurgence over the past two years has helped remind everyone how special Wrigley Field can be when the games matter, and Pete Crow-Armstrong's push for NL MVP has added a new layer of excitement for the home crowd. If the Cubs want to give that special crowd a chance to shine in October, beating the Phillies for the top wild-card spot is the priority.

Get Aaron Judge back in the lineup — and in the outfield — ASAP. The Yankees have treaded water just fine without their captain, but their ceiling in October is largely predicated on Judge's availability and impact . And getting Judge back from his rib injury isn't just about rejuvenating the lineup with a three-time MVP; it's also about assessing how the entire offense takes shape around him, especially if he needs days at DH as he eases back into action. Even if Giancarlo Stanton is out of the picture due to injury, Luis Garcia Jr., Ben Rice and Paul Goldschmidt make for a crowded 1B/DH depth chart, meaning Judge will need to resume right-field duties quickly to ensure the position-player group can function against both lefties and righties.

Get fully healthy on offense. Just as Roman Anthony and Trevor Story returned to the lineup after missing multiple months, Willson Contreras — by far the Sox's best hitter this season — landed on the injured list due to hamstring tightness . While that ailment isn't considered serious, it's frustrating that we've yet to see this lineup at full strength. That includes deadline additions Adley Rutschman, who is still looking to find his footing in Boston, and Curtis Mead, who is working his way back after suffering a fractured wrist in his first game with the Sox. What does this offense look like with everyone available? Hopefully we find out before October.

Clinch a wild-card spot. If the Padres qualify for the postseason, it would be their fifth trip to October in the past seven seasons — the same number of playoff appearances the franchise made from its inception in 1969 to 2019. It would also mark the first time in franchise history that they reached the postseason in three consecutive years. The expanded playoff field has a lot to do with these fun facts, of course, but it's still a reminder of what general manager AJ Preller and former owner Peter Seidler built — and why new owners Kwanza Jones and Jose E. Feliciano are so enthusiastic about getting involved. A return to October is not guaranteed, however. The division rival D-backs will have something to say, and the Padres will have to earn it.

Win the AL Central. Two years ago, the White Sox arrived in September having already lost 106 games. Last season, Chicago had the worst record in the American League by more than 10 games going into the final month. And look at them now . Already one of the great glow-ups in recent memory, this remarkable story is far from finished. The White Sox have a real shot at not only a division crown but also a first-round bye that would ensure a week of rest and a pair of home games to open the ALDS. What a world.

Clinch a wild-card spot. As the Ketel Marte saga lingers , the Snakes remain entranched in a heated wild-card race. If Arizona can keep pace with San Diego in September, as it has for much of the summer, it could lead to the juiciest series of the regular season's final weekend: D-backs at Padres for three games at Petco Park, potentially to determine the final NL wild-card spot. That would be fun!

Win the AL West. It sure hasn't been pretty — just ask fired general manager Dana Brown — but a clear opportunity remains for the Astros to reclaim the AL West crown after last year's postseason miss. In fact, a path still exists to a first-round bye if Houston can find some momentum. The Astros made meaningful progress in that effort by taking the series opener on Monday against the White Sox, their top competition for the No. 2 seed in the AL bracket.

Ride a José Ramirez hot streak to a postseason berth. It took 31 games for Ramirez to hit a home run after coming back from his broken hamate bone on July 22, but the star third baseman might be heating up just in time to propel Cleveland to a playoff berth for the third consecutive year. To this point, it has been the rookies — Parker Messick, Chase DeLauter, Travis Bazzana — fueling the Guardians, but now it's time for the future Hall of Famer to say, " Get in losers – we're going back to October."

Play well enough to give the final road trip real stakes. As the other fringe NL wild-card contenders have started to fade away, the Fightin' Fish just won't quit, staying at or above .500 for all of August. FanGraphs has Miami's playoff odds fading fast (2.3%) entering the final month, but the schedule offers an intriguing opportunity if the Marlins can avoid falling further: Their final road trip Sept. 14-24 takes them to the D-backs, Padres and Cubs — three of the four teams ahead of them in the wild-card standings. That could be a fun stretch if the Marlins can win enough games before then.

Clinch the final wild-card spot. Colton Cowser's mind-blowing, game-ending home run robbery to get the Orioles back to .500 for the first time since they were 15-15 on April 30 almost felt like a sign from the baseball gods that this team needs to be taken seriously. That said, the road to October is daunting for Baltimore, and the Orioles' six games remaining against Toronto will likely determine their fate. Still, considering the bleak state of affairs at the end of June, when the O's were 39-48 and five games out of the wild-card picture, vibes are pretty good with 24 games to go.

Clinch the final wild-card spot. The Blue Jays also entered the final month on a high note, with an emphatic sweep of Seattle. Now another marquee matchup in Cleveland awaits this week and will further clarify Toronto's chances of returning to October. It's hard to fully shake the letdown this season has been compared to the sky-high hopes coming in, but at this point, all the Blue Jays can do is make the most of the chances still ahead of them and push for another memorable October in this mediocre American League.

Return to October for the first time since winning the World Series. Texas should not be discounted in the underwhelming AL standings, though losing the tiebreaker against the Astros makes a late push for the division unlikely. That said, the Rangers could sneak in via the wild-card with a strong September, and it's safe to say no one would be excited to face Jacob deGrom in a best-of-three series. That's to say nothing of October darling Joc Pederson, who hasn't appeared in a postseason game since he won the World Series with Atlanta in 2021.

Finish above .500. Owners of the National League's longest postseason drought (2015), the Pirates' playoff odds per FanGraphs climbed as high as 62% at the start of June but have since plummeted toward zero, meaning another quiet October in Pittsburgh is in store. That's an awfully tough pill to swallow for this long-suffering fan base, and this might not be much of a consolation, but there's still a path for the Pirates to finish with a winning record, which they haven't done since 2018. Whether that'd be enough to save general manager Ben Cherington's job is unclear, but it would at least feel like progress. Also: If Paul Skenes can finish strong after an uncharacteristic midsummer dip in dominance, that would help lend optimism for 2027.

Finish strong enough to be taken seriously next year. As late as June 23, the Cardinals had the fourth-best record in the National League behind the Brewers, Braves and Dodgers. That strong first half suggested this wasn't the transition year many expected from the Cardinals, but their middling play more recently indicates that St. Louis wasn't quite ready for prime time. Can the Cards' young players show enough in September to restore some hype entering next season?

Let the kids play. This is the same goal I gave Minnesota in this exercise last year, but that was largely focused on the prospects acquired in their epic trade deadline sell-off. This year, another wave of young talent has arrived in the form of homegrown hitters such as Kaelen Culpepper and Walker Jenkins, with perhaps more on the way in Emmanuel Rodriguez, all of whom could anchor the Twins' lineup for years to come.

Take advantage of the schedule to embark on a miracle run. Making a late push to seize the title of Most Disappointing Team from the Mets, the Mariners have been a miserable watch lately by any standard — and especially for a team with their lofty preseason expectations. But you couldn't draw up a more favorable finish to the schedule, as Seattle plays 17 of its final 22 games against the three worst teams in baseball: seven against the Angels, seven against the A's and three against the Rockies. Is that soft slate enough to save the Mariners? Considering the hole they've dug for themselves, we shouldn't count on it.

Finish strong on the mound. With the Tarik Skubal homecoming behind them — and the chances of rallying to a wild-card spot evaporating daily — it's important for the Tigers to end this season on a positive note, pitching-wise, as they prepare for the post-Skubal era. Troy Melton has been one positive development this season, and it would be good to see more steadiness from veteran Framber Valdez, a meaningful step forward from 24-year-old Jackson Jobe and, perhaps most importantly, the Tigers debut of the top arm acquired in the Skubal trade, River Ryan. A proper send-off for Justin Verlander would also be nice.

Don't lose 90 games. The Nationals have made real strides this season under their new coaching staff and front office, but their poor form in recent weeks leaves them at risk of losing 90-plus games for a sixth consecutive season. Washington has the fewest games remaining of any ballclub, with 22 contests left, but that should be enough chances for them to notch the seven wins necessary to avoid the 90-loss mark.

Get Sal Stewart his hardware. Only four franchises (Dodgers, Yankees, Braves, A's) have produced more Rookies of the Year than the Reds, who have celebrated eight top-ranked rookies over the years and might have a ninth in Stewart, MLB's RBI leader and home run leader among rookies. St. Louis' JJ Wetherholt landing on the injured list clears the path somewhat for Stewart, but he'll still need to beat the Mets' duo of Nolan McLean and Carson Benge to clinch the award. Let's see if he can turn his dream into reality.

Play spoiler. This obviously was not the plan for September when the season began, but the Mets have played much better since deconstructing their pitching staff at the trade deadline and could make life difficult for a pair of rivals down the stretch. A three-game set at Yankee Stadium and a four-game home series against the Phillies represent golden opportunities for the Mets to sour the vibes for those postseason-bound clubs and perhaps even damage their position in the standings.

Enjoy a late push for MVP from Bobby Witt Jr. A sizable deficit in offensive production plus Kansas City's lackluster showing in the standings has kept Witt somewhat on the outside of the AL MVP conversation. But it's worth noting that Witt has a solid lead over Alvarez in WAR , thanks to his spectacular defense at shortstop, and a chance to lead the AL in stolen bases. Could a monster final month at the plate paired with a cold spell from Alvarez fuel Witt to MVP honors? It's unlikely, based on Alvarez's consistency, but it can't be ruled out.

Complete a (real) sweep. By beating the Braves in Monday's makeup game, the Giants technically swept Atlanta in all three games of their two-part visit to Truist Park, having won the first two games back in June before the finale was rained out. But other than that, San Francisco has failed to sweep a continuous series this season, which is a rather astonishing and rare shortcoming, even for a bad team. Eight series remain for Tony Vitello and the Giants to change that.

Don't lose 100 games. The Angels narrowly avoided losing 100 games for the first time in franchise history two years ago, winning their 63rd game on Sept. 22. Can they find 10 more wins over their final 24 games to repeat the feat and duck the unique ignominy of triple-digit losses? We'll see. It doesn't help that 15 of their remaining contests are on the road.

Find a new head of baseball operations. By parting with longtime baseball ops head David Forst in early August , the A's afforded themselves more time before the offseason to survey the front-office landscape and identify the best candidates to lead the organization as it prepares to move to Las Vegas in 2028. Whoever that individual turns out to be has a ton of work to do to get this franchise headed in the right direction after an injury-ravaged and non-competitive campaign, so the sooner they can take over, the better.

Don't lose 100 games. Unlike the Angels, the Rockies have lost 100 games before — each of the past three seasons, after avoiding such a fate for the first 30 years of the franchise's existence. Only four teams in MLB history have lost 100 games in four consecutive seasons. The Rockies need to notch 11 wins over their final 24 games to avoid becoming the fifth.

articles.title: Ketel Marte booed in return to Arizona after declining to deliver a message to Diamondbacks fans
articles.summary: Ketel Marte was met with boos in his return to the Diamondbacks lineup against the Phillies after his unexplained absence during the playoff race.
articles.body: As the 2026 Major League Baseball season somehow draws to a close, one of the most bizarre and inexplicable stories is the saga of Arizona Diamondbacks star Ketel Marte. Marte, long one of the best players in baseball and a pivotal part of a team pushing for a wild card spot, decided not to show up to a game between the Diamondbacks and Boston Red Sox at Fenway. He didn't tell anyone, including his teammates, manager, front office or coaching staff, that he wouldn't be at the ballpark. Didn't have a solid excuse ready, or a solid explanation, other than revealing a few days later that he was going for an MRI on his knee. His manager, Torey Lovullo, admitted that he felt "betrayed" by Marte's absence, and his teammates were clear that they also did not appreciate the fact that he didn't show up. The Diamondbacks' front office was also disappointed, saying it was a "complete mystery" and that the entire incident was "bizarre." KETEL MARTE'S UNEXPLAINED ABSENCE GETS STRANGER AS DIAMONDBACKS FIGHT FOR NL WILD CARD SPOT Marte eventually met with Lovullo and team executives at Chase Field in Phoenix, apologizing for his behavior and reaffirming his commitment to the team. And on Monday night, he finally made his return to the dugout as the Diamondbacks start a big series against the Philadelphia Phillies. Before the game, Marte answered questions from the media, including one in which he addressed how he'd handle speaking to the rest of the clubhouse. DIAMONDBACKS STAR SPOTTED AT CASINO DURING TEAM'S GAME AFTER NO-SHOWING TO STADIUM EARLIER IN THE WEEK "I'm going to stand in front of my teammates like a man," he said. "I'm going to ask for forgiveness. We're human, we all commit mistakes." As for what happened to lead to Marte's unexcused absence? Well, that's still unclear. "A moment of frustration," he explained. "No one made the decision for me, I'm the one that made the decision to not show up. I get along really well with Torey, and in that instance I failed him by not showing up," he added. Given that Marte missed so much time during a playoff race, fans were always going to have a difficult time accepting his absence. He was asked about that too, whether he had a message for the Diamondbacks' fan base after what happened, but Marte shook his head without giving an explanation. Well, those same fans clearly weren't thrilled about it. When Marte came up to the plate for his first at-bat, he was met with a chorus of boos. Boos that got louder after he grounded out in his first plate appearance. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! After the game, Marte explained that he hadn't understood the phrasing of the question asking what he'd like to say to the fans. "Going back to the press conference, when the question was made to me, I didn’t really quite understand the word that was used at that moment," he said. "I’m never going to stop loving my fans, and that’s what I want them to understand." English isn't Marte's first language, and he relies on an interpreter to talk to the media, so it's very possible he didn't fully understand the question. But his hat choice for postgame media availability raised some eyebrows and gave some cause to doubt whether that explanation was fully accurate. "May the bridges I burn light the way" is certainly a choice for someone who missed two weeks' worth of games late in the season. Marte has missed games in the past, and it's very possible that there are other mental health issues at work here, not to mention potential off-the-field problems. Supporting someone as they deal with off-field problems, personal issues, or other family concerns is part of fandom and sports in general. It’s hard, though, for fans to have grace when they aren’t given much explanation, justification or apology. articles.title: Mike Trout Checked with Rams Players About Stan Kroenke After Angels Sale amid Trade Speculation
articles.summary: Los Angeles Angels star Mike Trout attempted to do some recon on Stan Kroenke following the franchise's proposed sale.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Angels star Mike Trout attempted to do some recon on Stan Kroenke following the franchise's proposed sale.

The Angels announced Tuesday that Kroenke is purchasing a controlling stake from Arte Moreno. Trout and teammate Zach Neto reached out to some players on the Los Angeles Rams, another team owned by Kroenke, to gain insight into how he runs things:

5 Things That Could Derail NYY Title Run 😱

ESPN's Buster Olney posted that Kroenke's arrival, which is expected in early 2027, could have a significant impact on the Angels' on-field fortunes. That, in turn, could influence whether Trout finishes his career in L.A.:

"Trout always has the option to try to force his way off the Angels, and a new owner is more likely to consider that path than Moreno, who was never going to trade a future inner-circle Hall of Famer and the face of his franchise — and so that could now be a more viable option. If Trout stays — and that seems more likely — then the Angels are bound to be more effectively run going into the future. Let's put it more bluntly: It's impossible for Kroenke to run baseball operations worse than Morena has during Trout's career."

Moreno bought the Angels in 2003. He benefited from the general wave of positivity stemming from the franchise's 2002 World Series title. He also built goodwill by lowering prices for fans and investing big in the roster.

Moreno has overseen a period in which the Angels reached the playoffs once since 2009. Their prolonged futility, despite having generational stars such as Trout and Shohei Ohtani, became a running joke among baseball fans.

It's tough to imagine the ownership situation getting worse, hence the excitement surrounding Kroenke.

The 79-year-old can also point to a track record of his teams winning championships. The Rams claimed a pair of titles, and the same goes for the NHL's Colorado Avalanche. The Denver Nuggets won the NBA Finals for the first time in 2023. The Arsenal men's team is the reigning Premier League champion, and the Arsenal Women were the European champions in 2024-25.

Of course, Kroenke probably remains persona non grata in the state of Missouri after orchestrating the Rams' move to Los Angeles from St. Louis in 2016.

That's unlikely to be a problem for the Angels. While they're overshadowed by their neighbors to the north, they're not leaving Anaheim anytime soon.

The Angels' on-field product should start to improve. As it relates to Trout, the question is whether that happens quickly enough to capitalize on his post-peak years when he remains a productive player.

articles.title: Arte Moreno era officially over as Angels sell to Rams owner Stan Kroenke for $4B
articles.summary: Stan Kroenke agreed to buy the Angels from Arte Moreno for north of $4 billion, making it the single most expensive franchise sale in MLB history.
articles.body: Calling all Angels fans: The Arte Moreno era is officially over. After two decades of blown leads, wasted talent, and front-office chaos, Moreno has finally done what Halos fans have begged him to do for years: Arte finally agreed to sell the team. Billionaire Stan Kroenke, owner of the Rams, Nuggets and Avalanche, swooped in Tuesday to rescue the Angels from baseball’s purgatory. Kroenke Sports & Entertainment is buying the franchise for $4 billion — making it the most expensive sale in Major League Baseball history. PADRES STRIKE DEAL TO SELL TO INVESTOR GROUP LED BY PRIVATE EQUITY BILLIONAIRE, VOWS WORLD SERIES CHAMPIONSHIP "The Angels are a storied franchise anchored in a great market," Kroenke announced in a statement. "We look forward to an exciting future with the Angels organization." The price tag eclipses the Padres’ $3.9 billion record and crushes Steve Cohen’s $2.4 billion purchase of the Mets. MLB ALL-STAR MIKE TROUT SHUTS DOWN IDEA OF LEAVING LA, SAYS DOUBTERS FUEL PUSH TO GET ANGELS BACK TO PLAYOFFS Across American sports, it matches Mat Ishbia’s $4 billion Phoenix Suns takeover, trailing only the Denver Broncos ($4.65 billion) and Washington Commanders ($6.05 billion). Moreno bought the club in 2003 for $184 million, right after its lone World Series title. He released a statement on the sale: "The Moreno Family has been honored to steward the Angels for 23 years, and we believe with KSE’s experience and success they are the best next owner for the franchise. "The Angels organization looks forward to continuing its commitment to the fans, our employees, the players and our business partners." KHOSLA FAMILY REACHES DEAL TO BUY SUPER BOWL CHAMPION SEAHAWKS FOR NFL-RECORD PRICE: REPORT The Halos haven't made the playoffs since 2014, the longest active postseason drought in baseball. Around baseball, the Halos became an absolute punchline for squandering the prime years of Mike Trout and Shohei Ohtani on the exact same roster. Ohtani eventually left, crossing town to win a World Series with the Dodgers, while Trout stayed behind, loyal to a fault. Under Moreno, the organization handed out disastrous contracts to aging stars like Albert Pujols, Josh Hamilton and Anthony Rendon, let the farm system rot, and constantly burned through leadership, most recently firing GM Perry Minasian in June. Then came the cruelest tease of all: Moreno’s 2023 decision to explore a sale, only to abruptly yank the team off the market citing "unfinished business." Through every bad contract and lost season, Halos fans kept packing Angel Stadium, proving how deeply beloved this team remains. That loyalty is why Tuesday turned into an impromptu party outside Angel Stadium. Hours before first pitch against the Yankees, fans gathered to celebrate Arte’s exit, like they’d just won a World Series. The Angels enter a new era under Kroenke, whose championship empire spans the Super Bowl-winning Rams, NBA champion Nuggets and Stanley Cup champion Avalanche. The deal won't officially close until early 2027, pending MLB approval, but the Moreno era is finished. articles.title: Mike Trout Reacts to Stan Kroenke Buying Angels from Arte Moreno, Felt 'It Was Needed'
articles.summary: Mike Trout is ready for the next chapter of the Los Angeles Angels.
articles.body:
Mike Trout is ready for the next chapter of the Los Angeles Angels.

After Stan Kroenke agreed to purchase the American League West team from Arte Moreno for what Bill Shaikin of the Los Angeles Times reported will be more than the MLB record of $3.9 billion, the veteran told reporters he thought the sale "was needed."

He added, "No hard feelings to Arte. But I'm super excited. The guys are excited. There's a good vibe around the clubhouse, vibe around the stadium. We're all excited."

Jazz Chisholm responds to Red Sox broadcaster's comments

Moreno has explored selling the Angels in the past but ended that process in January 2023. He purchased the organization for $182.5 million in 2003.

As for Kroenke, he is quite familiar with franchise ownership.

He holds ownership stake in the Los Angeles Rams, Denver Nuggets, Colorado Avalanche, Colorado Rapids, Colorado Mammoth, and Arsenal men's and women's teams. He is now entering the Major League Baseball space and taking over a team that has struggled as Moreno's tenure continued.

The Angels were the reigning World Series champions when Moreno purchased them in 2003 and proceeded to make the postseason five times in a six-year span from 2004 through 2009. While they never advanced past the American League Championship Series, they were among the most consistent teams in the league.

But that has not been the case for more than a decade.

Los Angeles has made the playoffs just one time since 2009, and that was when it was swept in the 2014 AL Division Series.

Trout has been the face of the franchise for much of his career since he entered the majors in 2011. His resume includes three AL MVPs, an AL Rookie of the Year, nine Silver Slugger awards and 12 All-Star selections.

However, postseason success has not come with all of those individual accolades with Moreno owning the team.

Perhaps a change of ownership will bring more playoff appearances for the Angels, and Trout is looking forward to the next era.

articles.title: With MLB-record $4 billion sale, a brighter day is dawning for the Angels
articles.summary: The Angels, owned by Arte Moreno since 2003, have been in desperate need of an organizational facelift for a while.
articles.body:
Who says miracles don't come to Southern California?

Longtime Los Angeles Angels owner Arte Moreno shocked the baseball world on Tuesday, announcing the sale of the majority stake in the franchise to billionaire Stan Kroenke . Kroenke, who is also the owner of the Los Angeles Rams, Denver Nuggets, Colorado Avalanche, Colorado Rapids, Colorado Mammoth (of the National Lacrosse League) and Arsenal Football Club, already boasts one of the greatest ownership portfolios in sports.

With the purchase of the Angels, Kroenke becomes the sport's richest owner, passing New York Mets owner Steve Cohen in terms of estimated net worth. Moreno reportedly sold the franchise to Kroenke Sports & Entertainment for an MLB-record $4 billion . Earlier this month, the San Diego Padres finalized the sale of the team to husband-and-wife duo José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones for $3.9 billion , then an MLB record.

For the Angels, the sale has the potential to be massively impactful because this franchise has been in desperate need of an organizational facelift for a while. When Moreno bought the team in 2003, there was optimism surrounding the franchise, with the team coming off a World Series victory in 2002. In Moreno's first seven years as majority owner, the team remained one of the AL's best, making five postseason appearances.

But since 2010, Moreno's ownership had left much to be desired. With just one playoff appearance in that span — an ALDS sweep at the hands of the Royals in 2014 — the Angels have become one of the laughingstocks of baseball. And as the crosstown Dodgers have grown into a global brand over the past several years, the Angels have diminished from laughable to irrelevant.

As the Angels stopped being successful on the field, organizational problems gradually became exposed. With a deteriorating ballpark and a team that consistently finished at the bottom of the standings, it became clear that attention to detail was no longer one of Moreno's priorities. It also became apparent that Los Angeles was behind the times in the front office infrastructure as it relates to analytics. And while Moreno would occasionally invest in the roster, unsuccessful free-agent outlays — notably for Albert Pujols, Josh Hamilton and Anthony Rendon — left the team in a difficult position financially.

The lack of consistency within the organization is evidenced by the team's four general managers since 2011 and five managers since 2019, two revolving doors that never gave the operation a chance to find a consistent voice in the front office or in the dugout. The team never entered full rebuild mode, yet never seemed to have the pieces to truly contend. What's more, Moreno's harsh demeanor and demanding style built a reputation as arguably the most difficult person to work for in the sport.

Yet the greatest indictment of Moreno and the headline for his legacy will be his failure to build a winning team around two of the greatest players baseball has ever seen in Mike Trout and Shohei Ohtani. The two all-time greats played together in Anaheim for six seasons from 2018 to 2023 — and reached the postseason a grand total of zero times, an organizational failure that is difficult to comprehend even now.

One of the biggest complaints going into the expiration of the current CBA in December and negotiations for the next one is that there aren't enough baseball owners who care about winning.

Well, regardless of the sport, Kroenke's commitment to winning has always been apparent and effective. Nearly every franchise he owns — the Rams, the Avalanche, the Nuggets, the Rapids, the Mammoth and Arsenal — has won at least one championship under his stewardship. When it comes to the new Angels owner, not only has winning become the norm, it has also become his legacy with every franchise he puts his stamp on.

For the better part of the past 15 years, Angels fans have had little to be excited about. Even the greatness of Trout and Ohtani was overshadowed by the fact that the organization's ineptitude kept the two MVPs from fulfilling their potential in Anaheim.

But Kroenke's arrival brings an overnight change from what has been a series of dark chapters, and suddenly, the Angels' future is brighter than it has been in 20 years.

articles.title: Pirates score wild 13-12 win over Giants on walk-off error despite 5 ER allowed by Paul Skenes, blown 5-run lead
articles.summary: This is one way to win a ball game.
articles.body:
If you had seen at the beginning of the season that the San Francisco Giants were starting Logan Webb and the Pittsburgh Pirates were countering with Paul Skenes, you would have popped some popcorn to watch a duel between aces.

Instead, both had subpar outings Tuesday as the Pirates secured a wild 13-12 win in extra innings on a walk-off error.

The Pirates appeared in control of the game late despite five earned runs allowed by Skenes, the reigning Cy Young winner in the National League. They took a 12-7 lead into the eighth thanks in large part to nine earned runs allowed by Webb.

But Pirates relievers Evan Sisk and Luke Weaver combined to allow five earned runs in a top of the eighth that featured four consecutive walks followed by a double and a single. This allowed the Giants to tie the game 12-12, a score that stood heading into the bottom of the ninth inning. But the Giants couldn't capitalize on their good fortune.

The game ended in fitting fashion, with a botched throw on a two-out Rafael Flores Jr. ground ball and that allowed Pirates second baseman Brandon Lowe to score the game-winning run on an error. Osleivis Basabe's throw was too low and scooted past first base.

This resulted in a celebratory water-bucket bath for Flores due to his should-have-been third-out ground ball that instead allowed the game-winning run to score. Because why not.

The game was a fiasco for both teams long before the late-inning shenanigans.

Skenes vs. Webb was hardly a pitchers' duel

Skenes got out of the top of the first inning unscathed but had a brutal second. He started with a leadoff walk, then allowed an infield single. After a sacrifice bunt, Skenes gave up back-to-back RBI singles and then a three-run home run to Rafael Devers. In total, the Giants scored five in the frame.

The Pittsburgh ace worked a clean third and fourth inning but was pulled with two outs in the fifth with his pitch count at 95.

Skenes entered the game with a 9-11 record and a 3.79 ERA. With the five earned runs Tuesday, his ERA increased to 3.97. The former NL Rookie of the Year and NL Cy Young winner hasn't finished a season with an ERA over 2.00 but is almost guaranteed to do so this year, barring some lights-out performances before the end of the regular season.

While Skenes' day was rough, Webb's was outright bad.

The Giants ace allowed two earned runs in the bottom of the first inning on RBI singles from Nick Gonzales and Oneil Cruz. Webb then pitched a clean second before imploding in the third.

He allowed four consecutive singles and then issued back-to-back walks with the bases loaded. After one more RBI single, he was pulled from the game with the bases loaded and no outs.

Braxton Roxby came out of the pen, and two more runs for which Webb was responsible crossed the plate.

The right-hander's final stat line for the game was 2-plus innings pitched and 9 earned runs allowed on 9 hits and 2 walks. He threw only 65 pitches. It was the most earned runs he had ever allowed in a start, and it was the second-shortest outing of his career.

Webb entered the game with a 3.72 ERA, but after the dismal outing, that increased to 4.21. If his ERA stays above 4.0, it will be the first time he has had an ERA above 3.65 since 2020.

The lone bright spot for both pitchers is that the game descended into utter chaos after they left, and neither was saddled with the loss.

Pittsburgh leaves the game with 68-71 record, good for fourth place in the NL Central. San Francisco leaves at 57-82 record, ahead of only the Colorado Rockies in the NL West.

articles.title: Ketel Marte Explains 'Burning Bridges' Hat Choice After Viral Photo From Diamondbacks Return
articles.summary: Arizona Diamondbacks veteran Ketel Marte said Tuesday he wasn't fully aware of the meaning of the message that said "may the bridges I burn light the way" on the hat he wore Monday.
articles.body:
Arizona Diamondbacks veteran Ketel Marte said Tuesday he wasn't fully aware of the meaning of the message that said "may the bridges I burn light the way" on the hat he wore Monday.

"I didn't know what it was," he told Johnny Flores Jr. of The Athletic. "... I didn't know I had that hat on. I didn't know, I just put it on."

Flores explained that Marte's first language is Spanish and he uses an interpreter for interviews. The comments came after he was read a direct translation of the message on the hat.

The hat certainly made headlines considering he was away from the Diamondbacks for 13 games after he did not show up at Fenway Park for a game against the Boston Red Sox last month. Arizona initially placed him on the restricted list for three games before moving him to the injured list due to inflammation in his left knee.

He told reporters Monday he was going to apologize to his teammates and said, "We're human, we all make mistakes."

The story made more headlines when he was away from the team and seen at a casino when the Diamondbacks were playing a game, although manager Torey Lovullo said Marte was "free to do whatever he wants" as long as he was completing his rehab work.

On Tuesday, Lovullo said, "I want to move past this Ketel stuff as quickly as possible. I think if you chop up those words, maybe he's taking some accountability. He feels like he's done some things, and he wants to get better. That's how I read it."

Arizona is tied with the San Diego Padres for the final wild-card spot in the National League, so it is surely hoping to receive a much-needed boost from Marte's return.

The three-time All-Star and two-time Silver Slugger played designated hitter and hit fourth in the lineup for Tuesday's game against the Philadelphia Phillies.

articles.title: 10 Things We Think Will Happen Before the 2026 MLB Playoffs
articles.summary: With less than four weeks remaining until the start of Major League Baseball's 2026 postseason, the sprint to the finish line has officially begun.
articles.body:
With less than four weeks remaining until the start of Major League Baseball's 2026 postseason, the sprint to the finish line has officially begun.

Clinching countdowns, elimination numbers and surely a convoluted tiebreaking scenario or two will be all the rage throughout September, per usual.

Before we can completely set our sights on October, though, what are some of the things we expect to happen over the course of this final month of the regular season?

Will Pete Crow-Armstrong reach the 40/40 plateau? Does Shohei Ohtani pitch again? Can Yordan Alvarez lock up the Triple Crown? And who does secure those final few spots in the postseason field?

These 10 predictions for the home stretch are presented in no particular order.

Toronto Stays Hot and Crashes the Postseason Party

On April 4, the Toronto Blue Jays lost to the Chicago White Sox, falling to 4-4 overall.

They haven't woken up to a winning record since.

Since slipping to 49-59 in late July, though, they have been one of the hottest teams in baseball at 19-11, punctuated by a sweep of the Seattle Mariners this past weekend.

They enter September just 1.5 games behind the Cleveland Guardians in a certified cluster of mediocrity for the AL's final wild card spot.

And wouldn't you know it, they open the month with a three-game set in Cleveland before closing out the regular season with 21 consecutive games against teams with .500 or worse records.

The starting rotation has been decimated by injuries, but can they take two out of three from the Guardians and then actually do something with that gift of a remaining schedule?

Brett Bateman has provided an unexpected boost, batting .333 since arriving in the Kevin Gausman trade. Alejandro Kirk has been hot over the past month, too. And George Springer has been on an absolute tear as of late, batting .487/.524/.769 over the last 12 games.

If they could just get Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and/or Ernie Clement going, they would be in business.

To that end, wouldn't it be something if Guerrero's first home run at Rogers Centre in 2026 was a walk-off blast that clinched the Blue Jays' spot in the postseason?

Dating back to August 11, 12 of Pete Crow-Armstrong's 22 hits have been home runs, bringing his season total to 38—just two behind Kyle Schwarber for the best mark in the majors.

During his recent explosion of five home runs in two games against the Reds, Cubs fans started to joke that he needs to quit hitting so many dingers because you can't steal bases when you're constantly trotting around them.

While there is, of course, some truth to that sentiment, PCA racked up 12 home runs and nine stolen bases in 26 games between June 3 and July 1 when he first caught fire. And Shohei Ohtani sure did prove two years ago with 54 home runs and 59 stolen bases that it's entirely possible to do both.

With 32 stolen bases to date and a very real chance to become just the seventh member of the exclusive 40/40 club, Crow-Armstrong is presumably going to have even more of a green light on the basepaths than usual, at least until he reaches that plateau.

At this point, it's not even a question of whether he'll get to 40 home runs, but rather a question of whether he could even get to 50.

Either way, the NL MVP race is effectively over now.

It could've gone either way between Crow-Armstrong and Ohtani as little as four days ago. But between PCA's rampage against Cincinnati's pitching and Ohtani's return to the mound getting postponed again, Shohei's streak of three straight MVPs is coming to an end.

Yordan Alvarez Completes the Triple Crown Quest...

At the end of July, Yordan Alvarez winning the Triple Crown was starting to look like a foregone conclusion. His .324 batting average was best in the American League by a 22-point margin. And with 35 home runs and 82 RBI, he had cushions of four and nine, respectively, in those races.

Unfortunately, he hit quite a wall in August, going through a 22-game stretch with just one home run, seven RBI and a .253 batting average.

All of a sudden, it's shaping up to be a three-way photo finish, tied with Junior Caminero for the most home runs, three RBI ahead of Pete Alonso for the lead in that department and just six points ahead of red-hot Chandler Simpson for the top batting average.

Over the course of his career, though, Alvarez has triple-slashed .306/.400/.600 in September.

Even last year, which was mostly a disastrous one for him, he still managed an OPS north of 1.000 for the 13 games he was able to play in September.

And he's going to do it again, rallying from a rough August to end up with a .319 batting average, 45 home runs and 115 RBI. He joins 2012 Miguel Cabrera as the only batting Triple Crowns since the 1960s and wins AL MVP unanimously.

...But Houston Misses Postseason on a Tiebreaker for Second Consecutive Year

After winning road series against the Yankees and Mets this past week, the Houston Astros are back above .500, entering play on Tuesday with a two-game lead over the Texas Rangers and a six-game edge over the Seattle Mariners.

But while the Astros are currently facing the White Sox and still have series remaining against Tampa Bay, Atlanta, Philadelphia, Arizona and Seattle, the Mariners' remaining schedule might be the most favorable closing stretch in MLB history.

After finishing up their current series in Boston, the M's have a homestand against the A's and Rangers, a road trip against the A's, Angels and Rockies and a final homestand against the Astros and Angels.

It's a 22-game run in which their opponents have a combined .408 winning percentage, and their only games against a .500-or-better foe are two home contests against the Astros, the team they are chasing for the AL West crown. Seattle has already gone 9-2 against Houston this season.

Though this Mariners team hasn't been even remotely as good as last year's squad was, let's not forget that they turned a 3.5-game deficit into a 5.0-game lead by reeling off 17 wins in 18 games (including a pivotal sweep of Houston) last September.

Both Houston and Seattle finish at 82-80—while Texas remains slightly below .500—and the Mariners win the division on a tiebreaker.

Notably, 82-80 should keep the Astros right in the mix for the final wild card spot. But either Toronto or Cleveland will edge them out at 83-79.

Dodgers Pull the Plug on Shohei Ohtani's Pitching Rehab

When Shohei Ohtani last took the mound on July 3, he was running away with the NL MVP and was easily a top five candidate for NL Cy Young Award.

If he had been able to keep it up for another three months, it would have gone down as the best two-way season of his career, on pace for a WAR north of 10.

Lately, though, Ohtani simply hasn't been Ohtani.

He played in every game in August, but posted a .795 OPS. And unless you want to count September 2023 when he only played in three games, that was his worst OPS in a calendar month since April 2022.

Maybe it's just a rare slump at the dish, unrelated to the left knee, right biceps and " overall body " soreness that has kept him from pitching in a game for nearly two months at this point.

Or maybe the pitching rehab is the main reason for the hitting regression?

Unless they can somehow definitively rule that out, Dave Roberts and the Dodgers' high-level decision makers need to start asking themselves if it's really worth it to continue with his pitching rehab.

After all, they already have (provided they stay healthy) a dynamite starting rotation for the postseason featuring Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, each with a sub-2.85 ERA for the year.

Would it be nice to get Ohtani back to the point where he can be a two-inning or three-inning opener before handing the baton to Glasnow?

It would also be wild if he could come back as their closer. However, using him in a relief capacity gets a bit messy, because they would lose him as their DH if they had to subsequently replace him with another reliever. Considering there were multiple marathon games in last year's World Series, they'll presumably be reluctant to go that route.

But especially with Andy Pages out indefinitely, the Dodgers need Ohtani's bat much, much more than they need his arm. They were averaging 5.4 runs per game and had a 58-31 record when he last pitched. Since then, they're at 4.0 and 24-24, respectively.

Milwaukee Brewers Re-Break Franchise Record for Wins in a Season, Earn No. 1 Seed Again

The funny thing about all this "The Dodgers are breaking baseball!" and "We need a salary cap to level the playing field!" outrage ahead of a virtually inevitable lockout is that the low-budget Milwaukee Brewers have the best record in baseball since the beginning of Los Angeles' reign of deferred contracts terror.

The Brew Crew were the No. 1 overall seed last year, and they are on track to get it again this year.

Better yet, if the season ended today, it would be Milwaukee (19th in tax payroll, per Spotrac ) and Tampa Bay (27th in tax payroll) as the No. 1 seeds—while the 62-76 Mets have an all-in cost (payroll plus tax bill) that is about $70M greater than what the division-leading Brewers, Rays and White Sox are paying combined .

The Brewers are 85-53, 2.5 games clear of the Dodgers for the top overall spot. They are on pace for 99.8 wins, and merely need to go 13-11 the rest of the way to break the franchise record for wins in a season—97, set in 2025.

They'll crack triple digits, though, finishing 100-62.

They've gone 22-12 within the NL Central thus far, and 18 of their remaining 24 games are against divisional foes. The six against the Cubs represent a challenge, but the other 12 are what will help keep them atop the standings when all is said and done.

White Sox Punctuate Unreal Bounce-Back Year with 1st-Round Bye

The Chicago White Sox have been in first place in the AL Central on a daily basis for nearly two months at this point, yet it's still hard to process how they've managed to turn things around as quickly as they have.

Just two years ago, they set the live ball era record for most losses in a single season, going 41-121. The pitching was a nightmare, aside from Garrett Crochet, who they traded away that winter. And at 3.13 runs per game, they had the lowest scoring offense in an MLB season since 1972.

Moreover, that disaster year came in the middle of a three-year streak of 100-plus losses. In MLB history, no team had won at least 71 games the year after such a run of ineptitude.

An entire factory of rose-colored glasses wouldn't have been enough to see this coming six months ago: Chicago is 72-65 and leading the American League in scoring.

The Guardians are three games back in the AL Central, with one major head-to-head series remaining. Chicago travels to Cleveland for a Sept. 14-16 clash.

But the White Sox otherwise have one of the easiest remaining schedules in the majors, while the Guardians aren't even being serious in their pursuit of the postseason, opting against using one of their September callup spots on Ralphy Velazquez—who hit .356/.433/.867 with 15 home runs in August—presumably because they want him to continue playing in the minors if there is a lockout, which players cannot do if they are on a 40-man roster.

Even if Cleveland had promoted its top prospect, though, the White Sox have had astounding staying power with Munetaka Murakami, Colson Montgomery and Miguel Vargas all on the brink of 30 home runs. They'll stay ahead and they'll secure the No. 2 seed.

Friday Night Determines Who Wins the NL East

Both Atlanta and Philadelphia enter September on a heater.

The Braves recently won seven in a row, including sweeping the Dodgers in what they hope was a pivotal series for first-round bye purposes. But the Phillies went 21-7 in August, climbing back to within striking distance at just four games behind Atlanta in the NL East.

Better yet, they have seven head-to-head games remaining, the first of which comes this Friday in Philadelphia, with a projected pitching matchup of Chris Sale vs. Cristopher Sánchez.

If Sale takes care of business like he did back in April in back-to-back wins over the Phillies (13.0 IP, 6 H, 1 R, 16 K), that might be all she wrote for this race. (Though, it would make things a wee bit more compelling in the NL Cy Young race.) Atlanta would be ahead 6-1 in the head-to-head series at that point, leaving the Phillies probably needing to win at least five of the remaining six to claw their way back.

But if it's Sánchez doing the shoving while the Phillies' bats get to Sale, that could be the beginning of a massive swing that bumps Atlanta out of first place in the NL East for the first time since early April.

In fact, we're going so far as to say the winner of Friday night's showdown ultimately wins the NL East. Pre-Labor Day games don't usually carry that much weight, but this one could.

Aaron Judge Returns Next Week, Albeit with Some Rust

Aaron Judge has not played since the end of May, slowly recovering from a stress fracture in his rib.

It has already been the longest IL stint of his career, but the Yankees are starting to see some light at the end of the tunnel. Judge accompanied the team on their current road trip, and there's a very real chance he'll return during next week's homestand against the Rockies and Mets.

Now that the "when" is close to being answered, the big question becomes how he'll look if he actually jumps right back in without a rehab assignment after more than three months on the shelf.

When he came back from a fractured wrist in mid-September 2018, he had a .675 OPS in 12 games played the rest of the way. (Though, he did hit .421/.500/.947 that postseason.)

It was a similar story in 2020 when he returned from a calf injury in mid-September and posted a .548 OPS down the stretch.

And when he missed nearly two months with a toe injury in 2023, he had a .685 OPS in his first nine games back before starting to turn things back around.

Basically, if you're expecting Judge to come back and go yard in three of his first 10 plate appearances, his history suggests you're going to be disappointed—even against the pitching staffs of the Rockies and Mets.

If he can lock back in after roughly two weeks, though, well, that'd be just in time for a massive four-game set against the Tampa Bay Rays, as well as just in time for the postseason.

Return of Joe Musgrove and Nick Pivetta Helps Propel Padres Into Postseason

The San Diego Padres have been waiting, waiting and waiting some more for two of their best pitchers to return from elbow/forearm injuries.

Nick Pivetta hasn't pitched in the majors since mid-April.

Joe Musgrove was last seen during the 2024 Wild Card Round.

But the former tossed 4.1 scoreless innings at Triple-A El Paso on Sunday, that coming three days after the latter allowed one run in five innings of work at the same level.

Each one reached 60 pitches and plausibly could make his next appearance in the majors.

No time like the present, too, locked in a dead heat with the Arizona Diamondbacks for the final NL wild card spot.

It's looking likely that the race will come right down to the wire, with the Padres hosting the Snakes over the final weekend of the regular season. San Diego can't afford to cede any more ground before then, though, so working Musgrove and Pivetta into the mix ASAP could be huge—especially if it ends in those two and Michael King being lined up to start during that massive final series.

How they would make it work remains to be seen. Probably a six-man rotation with one of Casey Mize, Randy Vásquez or Walker Buehler transitioning to a bulk relief role. But having too many healthy starting pitchers sure would be a new dilemma for the Padres after the past few years of seemingly never having a complete rotation.

articles.title: Ranking the Yankees' 10 Best Power Hitters of All Time
articles.summary: The most storied slugger in MLB history and the most prolific home run threat in the game today bookend the long history of power hitters wearing a New York Yankees uniform.
articles.body:
The most storied slugger in MLB history and the most prolific home run threat in the game today bookend the long history of power hitters wearing a New York Yankees uniform.

Between Babe Ruth and Aaron Judge, there have been some all-time greats who took their turn launching balls out of Yankee Stadium, and we've set out to identify the 10 best in franchise history.

Looking beyond just home run totals, at-bats per home run, total 30- and 40-homer seasons and reputation relative to the era they played in all played a role in determining the final list and order.

Before we get to the top 10, some honorable mentions are in order.

These players deserve a mention in any conversation of the Yankees' best power hitters, but they ultimately fell short of our final Top 10 list:

Yogi Berra — 358 total HR, sixth on NYY all-time list

Curtis Granderson — 40-HR seasons in 2011 and 2012

Charlie Keller — 153 OPS+, three 30-HR seasons

Don Mattingly — 222 total HR, three 30-HR seasons

Graig Nettles — 250 total HR, 1976 AL HR leader

Gary Sheffield — 30-HR/120-RBI seasons in 2004 and 2005

Alfonso Soriano — 30/30 seasons in 2002 and 2003

Juan Soto — 41 HR in only season with Yankees

Mark Teixeira — 2009 AL HR leader, four 30-HR seasons

Dave Winfield — 205 total HR, two 30-HR seasons

HR: 189 | AB/HR: 14.7 | HR High: 38 30-HR: 3 | 40-HR: 0 | 50-HR: 0

Despite his injury woes, Giancarlo Stanton has remained an impactful power hitter when he has been able to take the field for the Yankees, and it's easy to forget his tenure in the Bronx began with a 38-homer campaign that garnered MVP votes.

He also owns a .926 OPS and 18 home runs in 48 career playoff games, all of which have come in a Yankees uniform. Can he get back to a level of health that allows him to reach 500 home runs before his time with the team is over?

HR: 144 | AB/HR: 16.3 | HR High: 41 30-HR: 2 | 40-HR: 1 | 50-HR: 0

Reggie Jackson already had 281 home runs and an MVP award when he joined the Yankees as a free agent in 1977, but he had a profound impact on the organization during his five-year tenure.

He slugged an AL-leading 41 home runs in 1980 to finish runner-up in AL MVP balloting. However, his enduring legacy and the origin of his "Mr. October" moniker came from his performance in the 1977 World Series, when he had a three-homer game and five total long balls.

5 Things That Could Derail NYY Title Run 😱

HR: 203 | AB/HR: 14.8 | HR High: 61 30-HR: 3 | 40-HR: 1 | 50-HR: 1

Roger Maris was the gold standard for single-season home run production from his record-setting 61-homer season in 1961 until the legendary 1998 home run race between Mark McGwire and Sammy Sosa.

However, he was by no means a one-year wonder, as his memorable '61 campaign was sandwiched between a 39-homer, 112-RBI performance in 1960 that also earned him MVP honors and a 33-homer, 100-RBI year in 1962.

HR: 209 | AB/HR: 14.0 | HR High: 41 30-HR: 5 | 40-HR: 2 | 50-HR: 0

The Yankees signed Jason Giambi to a seven-year, $120 million deal prior to the 2002 season, and he promptly delivered back-to-back 41-homer seasons to begin his tenure with the club.

Injuries cut short his 2004 and 2007 seasons, but he reached 30 home runs in each of the other five years of that contract, largely delivering on the middle-of-the-order anchor expectations that came with that megadeal.

HR: 361 | AB/HR: 18.9 | HR High: 46 30-HR: 7 | 40-HR: 1 | 50-HR: 0

Perhaps best known for his legendary 56-game hitting streak, Joe DiMaggio was also a consistent power source who effectively bridged the gap in Yankees history between Lou Gehrig's retirement and Mickey Mantle's debut.

His career-high 46 home runs came in just his second big league season at the age of 22, and his final 30-homer campaign came 13 years later when he batted .301/.394/.585 with 32 home runs and 122 RBI in his second-to-last season in the big leagues.

HR: 351 | AB/HR: 15.9 | HR High: 54 30-HR: 8 | 40-HR: 2 | 50-HR: 1

The AL MVP winner in 2005 (173 OPS+, 48 HR, 130 RBI) and 2007 (176 OPS+, 54 HR, 156 RBI), Alex Rodriguez hit a staggering 268 home runs over his first seven seasons in a Yankees uniform.

Injuries and a full-season PED suspension led to his production dropping significantly after that initial burst, but he did rebound with a 33-homer performance at the age of 39 in his final full season in the majors.

HR: 493 | AB/HR: 16.2 | HR High: 49 30-HR: 10 | 40-HR: 5 | 50-HR: 0

While he spent much of his career overshadowed by teammate Babe Ruth from a power production standpoint, Lou Gehrig earned his own spot among the most prolific power hitters in the history of the sport.

Across the 11-year stretch from 1927 to 1937, he hit .350/.459/.659 for a 189 OPS+ and averaged 39 home runs and 154 RBI per season. He led the AL in home runs three different times, and he is one of only 20 players in MLB history with at least five 40-homer seasons.

HR: 536 | AB/HR: 15.1 | HR High: 54 30-HR: 9 | 40-HR: 4 | 50-HR: 2

Mickey Mantle made his MLB debut at the age of 19, and by the time he reached his age-27 season, when most players are entering their prime, he already had 249 home runs, 61.4 WAR and two AL MVP awards.

He won the AL Triple Crown in 1956 (.353/52/130), and gave Roger Maris a run for his money during his historic 1961 season before ultimately finishing with 54 homers.

Mantle hit just 162 long balls in his 30s, but he had already solidified his status as one of the greatest to ever do it.

HR: 385 | AB/HR: 11.2 | HR High: 62 30-HR: 6 | 40-HR: 4 | 50-HR: 4

Mickey Mantle, Lou Gehrig and several other players behind him on this list have had more complete careers than Aaron Judge, who is still chasing his first World Series ring and shy of 400 career homers.

However, in terms of sheer power hitting production, Aaron Judge has earned the No. 2 spot on this list with a 62-homer peak, four 50-homer seasons and a ridiculous 11.2 AB/HR rate that puts him in lockstep with the No. 1 player on this list.

HR: 659 | AB/HR: 11.0 | HR High: 60 30-HR: 13 | 40-HR: 11 | 50-HR: 4

A host of sluggers have come and gone since Babe Ruth hung up his spikes, but what more really needs to be said about the man who almost single-handedly ushered in the Live Ball Era.

When he hit 54 home runs in his first season with the Yankees in 1920, it nearly doubled the previous single-season record, which he also held with his 29-homer performance the year before.

Those 54 homers were more than 14 of the league's other 15 teams hit combined, and it was just the start of a transcendent run that would make him one of the most revered athletes of all time.

The Atlanta Braves announced Tuesday that they have selected the contract of right-hander Blake Burkhalter and infielder Kyle Farmer. In addition, fellow right-hander Robert Suarez was transferred to the 60-day injured list.

articles.title: Angels Fans Chant Goodbye to Arte Moreno in Video After Historic $4B Sale to Stan Kroenke
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Angels' ownership change won't be official for at least a few more months, but some of their fans are already bidding adieu to Arte Moreno.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Angels' ownership change won't be official for at least a few more months, but some of their fans are already bidding adieu to Arte Moreno.

A chant of "Goodbye, Arte" started during Tuesday's 7-3 loss to the New York Yankees.

The Angels announced Tuesday that Moreno struck an agreement to sell the Angels to Stan Kroenke, who owns franchises across multiple sports leagues including the Los Angeles Rams and Arsenal FC. The deal is expected to go through in early 2027.
